about: Plain notes the First Steps runner shows under a compile error after Check: the first note whose match finds the run's first error. A note's $1, $2 are the match's groups; `code` in a note is shown as code. A run's first error is its first line and the help and note lines under it. A note with "page": true answers a message the page writes itself (tour-client.mjs), such as a run that times out, and has no example. Each example's first error must be matched by its own note before any other (vmhost/tour_lesson_notes_test.go). match is a regular expression that Go and JavaScript read alike.

notes.match: division by zero: the divisor is the literal 0
notes.note: Dividing by 0 has no answer, so Nomi stops it before your code runs.
notes.example:
fn odd(n: Int) -> Bool
    n % 0 == 1
end

notes.note: Nomi won't divide by a number that might be zero, since that has no answer. Name the number, check it first, and divide only when it isn't zero: `if count == 0 then ... else total / count`.

link.label: The lesson on decisions shows how

notes.example:
fn average(xs: List<Int>) -> Int
    Iter.sum(xs) / Iter.count(xs)
end

notes.note: A single `=` names a value. To compare two values, write `==`: `if $1 == ...`.
notes.example:
fn is_one(n: Int) -> Bool
    if n = 1 then True else False
end

notes.note: Your function takes `$1` but doesn't use it yet. Use `$1` in the function's body.
notes.example:
fn double(n: Int) -> Int
    4
end

notes.note: You named a value `$1` but never used it. Use it, or remove the line that names it.
notes.example:
fn double(n: Int) -> Int
    twice = n * 2
    n + n
end

notes.note: Nomi doesn't know the name `$1`. Check its spelling against the names your code already has.
notes.example:
fn double(n: Int) -> Int
    n * 2
end

fn triple(n: Int) -> Int
    doubel(n) + n
end

notes.note: `$1` has nothing called `$2`. Check its spelling.
notes.example:
fn total(xs: List<Int>) -> Int
    Iter.summ(xs)
end

notes.note: A number with no `d` after it isn't a Decimal. Write `19.99d`, not `19.99`, and `2d`, not `2`.

link.label: The lesson on types shows how

notes.example:
fn price() -> Decimal
    19.99
end

notes.note: This call gives the function $2 values, and it takes $1. The values go in the parentheses, separated by commas.
notes.example:
fn double(n: Int) -> Int
    n * 2
end

fn triple(n: Int) -> Int
    double(n, 3)
end

notes.note: Value number $1 in this call should be a `$2`, and it is a `$3`.
notes.example:
fn double(n: Int) -> Int
    n * 2
end

fn four() -> Int
    double("2")
end

notes.match: return type mismatch: expected \S+, got Iter<
notes.note: `Iter.map` and `Iter.filter` give back an Iter, a sequence that isn't a list yet. End the pipe with `|> Iter.to_list()`.

link.label: The lesson on pipes shows how

notes.example:
fn doubled(xs: List<Int>) -> List<Int>
    xs |> Iter.map(fn n -> n * 2)
end

notes.match: return type mismatch: expected \S+, got Maybe<
notes.note: This value might be missing, so it is a Maybe. Say what to give back when it is missing, with `Maybe.with_default`.

link.label: The lesson on missing values shows how

notes.example:
fn age(name: String) -> Int
    ages = {"Ada" => 36}
    Map.get(ages, name)
end

notes.note: The function promises to give back `$1`, the type after `->`, but this gives back `$2`.
notes.example:
fn greeting() -> String
    42
end

notes.match: `\S+` needs two values of one type, and these are (Int and Decimal|Decimal and Int|Float and Decimal|Decimal and Float)
notes.note: Write every number in a sum with Decimals with a `d` after it: `2d`, not `2`.

link.label: The lesson on types shows how

notes.example:
fn midpoint(a: Decimal, b: Decimal) -> Decimal
    (a + b) / 2
end

notes.match: `\S+` needs two values of one type, and these are (Int and Float|Float and Int)
notes.note: A whole number and a decimal are different types, and Nomi won't mix them. Write the whole number with a decimal point: `2.0`, not `2`.

link.label: The lesson on types shows how

notes.example:
fn midpoint(a: Float, b: Float) -> Float
    (a + b) / 2
end

notes.match: `\+` needs two values of one type, and these are (String and \w+|\w+ and String)
notes.note: To put a value into a piece of text, write it inside the quotes: `"n is ${n}"`.

link.label: The lesson on text shows how

notes.example:
fn describe(n: Int) -> String
    "n is " + n
end

notes.note: `==` compares two values of the same type, and this compares a `$1` with a `$2`. `1` is a number and `"1"` is text.
notes.example:
fn is_one(n: Int) -> Bool
    n == "1"
end

notes.note: An `if` that gives back a value needs an `else`, for when its test is false.

link.label: The lesson on decisions shows how

notes.example:
fn describe(t: Int) -> String
    if t < 10 then "cold"
end

notes.note: Write `then` between an `if`'s test and its value: `if n > 1 then "big" else "small"`.
notes.example:
fn size(n: Int) -> String
    if n > 1 "big" else "small"
end

notes.note: Every `fn`, and every `test`, ends with its own `end`.
notes.example:
fn double(n: Int) -> Int
    n * 2

notes.note: A `case` says what to do for every kind of `$1`, and this one leaves out $2.

link.label: The lesson on choosing by kind shows how

notes.example:
enum Light
    Red
    Yellow
    Green
end

fn next(light: Light) -> Light
    case light
        .Red -> .Green
        .Green -> .Yellow
    end
end

notes.match: an expression cannot be written at file level
notes.note: Code runs inside a function. Put it between `fn main()` and its `end`.
notes.example: dbg 1 + 2

notes.note: A loop whose step never reaches its `break` repeats forever. Check that each step moves toward the stop.

link.label: The lesson on repeating shows how
